item.title: Human skepticism and formal verification
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: I believe mathematical claims that are verified in Lean, but this is also basically an appeal to authority. From the perspective of methodological skepticism, I do not know that the results claimed by OpenAI are true until I have studied them and personally convinced myself that they are true.
item.content:encoded:
Benjamin Friedman, postdoctoral fellow at Université du Québec à Montréal (UQÀM)

Introduction

On October 6, 2026, the artificial intelligence company OpenAI released a github repository containing 722 articles claiming new results across a large variety of mathematical disciplines. According to OpenAI, their models worked for an average of three hours to achieve each of the results.

Of note here is the decision to list the author of each article simply as “OpenAI”. It is highly unusual in mathematical scholarship for a company to be considered the author of an article. The decision to have the mathematicians hired by OpenAI generate these results anonymously is clearly intentional, since the idea is to show off the creative powers of the company’s product.

More troubling is the idea that these problems are already considered “solved” the same day that they are released to the public, well before the mathematical community has had any opportunity to verify the solutions. Many of these articles were accompanied by Lean scripts, with the implicit justification that so long as the statement in the article corresponds to the type instantiated in the Lean script, the results are to be seen as true.

I argue in this piece that formal verification, including Lean, is a mechanized implementation of a skeptical posture that is essential to mathematical practice, but that a certificate of formal verification is an unsatisfying substitute for human skepticism. I conclude the essay by advocating for methodological skepticism as a practice that will help keep our field grounded amid the tumultuous changes brought about by AI systems.

Skepticism as a mathematical method

Before we can describe how Lean mechanizes skepticism, and why a Lean certificate on its own is not satisfying, we must first understand the role of skepticism in mathematical practice. The role of skepticism in mathematics is methodological. The titular method in Descartes’ influential 1637 work Discourse on the method of rightly conducting one’s reason and of seeking truth in the sciences is a methodological skepticism, in which one advances carefully towards truth, never accepting any fact unless entirely convinced of its veracity. Descartes likens knowledge without a firm foundation to a building “built on mud or on sand”. One might imagine a skeptical attack of one’s purported knowledge as analogous to a “stress-test” of the building’s stability. Is this claim really established beyond all doubt? Let me shake it and see whether it stands, or whether it all comes crashing down! Thus, in the Cartesian view we can be certain only of those matters which stand up to the highest degree of skeptical attack.

This degree of skepticism is much too stringent to be practical in most contexts. Indeed, Descartes points out that since our knowledge of the world is factored through sensory experiences, which may be compromised by an elaborate deception, we cannot apply this methodological skepticism to most worldly matters. However since our objects of inquiry are abstract, mathematicians have the rare luxury among thinkers of being able to apply Cartesian-level skepticism to achieve substantial results.

In his book Mathematica, the mathematician and writer David Bessis draws on the writings of Descartes, Grothendieck, Thurston and others to show that mathematical practice consists of two layers: an “official” mathematics, in which we use formal logic to deduce facts about abstract mathematical objects, and a “secret” mathematics, which is an imaginative mode of thought, in which one develops mental pictures and intuitions for mathematics. According to Bessis, one develops mathematical knowledge through interrogating and correcting one’s intuitions about mathematical objects, leading to greater understanding. Thus, methodological skepticism is directed inwardly in order to sharpen the clarity of one’s mental pictures.

To illustrate this, Bessis makes a geometric claim: A straight line can intersect a circle in at most two distinct points. By employing a modest degree of visual imagination, one can attempt to refute the claim by trying to visualize a line intersecting a circle in three distinct points. However in this attempt at refutation, one will become convinced of the claim.

This also explains why experienced mathematicians can seem to their junior colleagues like they have supernatural abilities. A couple of years ago I had the distinct fortune of getting to meet a famous and influential mathematician in my field. I was explaining to him a problem that I was working on at the time, and he very quickly isolated certain hypotheses that would be required. My advisor and I had in fact come to the same conclusion, but over the course of several months instead of over the course of one conversation. The remarkably quick, seemingly effortless realization is very impressive. It was certainly not, however, a result of him rapidly performing formal deductive arguments or symbolic manipulations in his head. Rather, if we accept Bessis’s model of mathematical practice, then the explanation would be that he has developed a deep intuition for these sorts of problems through sustained mental habits – namely the creation of mental pictures paired with the skeptical interrogation and refinement of those pictures – over many years.

There is another account of skepticism that is important in order to understand the role of formal verification. The philosopher Catarina Dutilh Novaes argues in her book The Dialogical Roots of Deduction that deductive reasoning is structured around a dialogue between a prover, who seeks to establish a claim, and a skeptic, who resists belief in the claim unless compelled. Despite being on opposing sides of the dialogue, both roles are essential to establishing an air-tight deductive argument.

This dialogue is core to mathematical practice. Sometimes the dialogue is implicit, such as when a mathematician writing down a proof anticipates the objections of a skeptical reader. At other times, the dialogue is explicit, such as when a colleague at a seminar presents an objection to a mathematician’s argument, to which that mathematician is now obliged to respond to the colleague’s satisfaction.

A routine part of my training as a mathematician has been defending claims I wanted to make against the challenges of my teachers. Did my teachers really disbelieve the claims that I was making? Maybe in those rare cases in which my claims were entirely original, or in which I was making a claim about a more obscure result. But my teachers’ skepticism was present even when I was presenting results from well within the canon of my field. It would be ridiculous to imagine that the Hodge decomposition theorem, a standard theorem of differential geometry, is doubted by any expert. Rather, this skepticism is methodological on the part of my teachers, these interrogations serving as probes of my understanding. This is in line both with Bessis’s account of skepticism as sharpening one’s intuitions, as well as with Dutilh Novaes’ dialogical model, in which they are playing the skeptical role in a dialogue.

Dialogue between humans, and in particular the application of skepticism, has been the basis by which mathematical truth has been established for thousands of years, until the advent of:

Formal verification

Lean 4 is a proof assistant, meaning that it does not generate proofs, but only checks a proof’s validity. The basic concept behind this verification is something called the Curry–Howard correspondence, or “proofs as programs”. The Curry–Howard correspondence is related to the branch of computer science known as type theory. A theorem corresponds to a type, while a valid proof of the theorem corresponds to an instance of the type. This is more complicated than the type theory that one would typically encounter in an introductory computer science class, in which one would learn that 00 and 613613 and −7-7 are instances of the type int\mathrm{int}, but it is the same idea.

The idea behind formal verification, that a mathematical proof can be presented as a computer program whose successful compilation corresponds to the proof’s validity, was somewhat unsavoury to me at first, perhaps because I was unsettled at the idea of human skepticism being replaced by a mechanized process. Nevertheless, I was reassured to find that the proponents of Lean were not arguing to replace human skepticism with formal verification, but instead arguing that Lean could serve as a strong additional test of a theorem’s validity.

Using Lean can be thought of as a technological implementation of the prover-skeptic dialogue, in which the user assumes the role of prover, while the skeptic role is mechanized. To illustrate this, here is some Lean code attempting to formalize the famous proof that there exists no rational number qq such that q2=2q^2 =2, a proof by contradiction:

The intro tactic on line 4 introduces, by way of contradiction, a rational number qq satisfying hq, which states that q2=2q^2=2. This is followed by my attempt at convincing Lean that we can substitute q=abq = \frac{a}{b} with a,ba,b in lowest terms into the equation q2=2q^2=2. This is all code that I wrote, so we are seeing only the “prover” side of the dialogue. Let’s see Lean’s response at line 11:

This “tactic state” describes Lean’s understanding of the proof at line 11, beginning with a list of statements which I have convinced Lean to accept, namely

  • that we have a rational number qq,
  • that we have q2=2q^2=2 (this is called hq),
  • that there is an integer aa equal to the numerator of qq and a natural number bb equal to the denominator of qq, and
  • that we can substitute q=abq=\frac{a}{b} into the equation q2=2q^2=2.

Since this is a proof by contradiction, the goal, which is the statement appearing after the ⊢\vdash symbol, is the statement False.

So far, so good. If I was presenting this proof in a lecture hall, then Lean would be an audience member who is following my reasoning and is satisfied by my argument up to this point. But when we get to line 14, where I attempt to show that the greatest common divisor (GCD) of aa and bb is equal to 11, an error message shows up:

Remember that theorems in this context are types, so when the error message says that there is a “type mismatch”, this means that the statement I claim to be proving is not accepted by Lean as being entirely justified. Returning to the lecture hall, we can imagine the audience member raising a hand and objecting.

“Benji,” I hear this audience member say. “You promised to prove to us that the GCD of aa and bb is equal to 11, but instead you proved that they are coprime! Thus, I don’t accept your line of reasoning!”

This scenario is absurd, because real life humans know well that two integers are coprime if and only if their GCD is 11. In fact, most people take this to be the definition of “coprime”. Lean takes a more general definition encoded in Mathlib: two elements a,ba, b of a ring RR are said to be coprime if the sum of the ideals generated by aa and bb is the entire ring:

⟨a⟩+⟨b⟩=R.\langle a \rangle + \langle b \rangle = R.

So if I wanted the error message to go away (that is, if I wanted to respond to the audience member’s objection to their satisfaction), I would have to prove that these two ways of looking at coprimality are equivalent in the ring of integers. This would not be difficult to do, but the point is that Lean gets hung up on these sorts of things all the time. The example here is a minutia with which no human mathematician would ever be bothered, but the argument put forth by proponents of Lean is that the process of formalizing a proof in Lean can sometimes result in important gaps being caught.

So we have seen that Lean is very good at being skeptical. This degree of skepticism is precisely the point of Lean, and why a Lean certificate grants a mathematical result a high degree of credibility.

OpenAI’s rapid advances are due to a mechanized prover-skeptic dialogue

Let us return now to the 722 results claimed by OpenAI. The spectacular rapidity with which the anonymous mathematicians at OpenAI have progressed is due to both roles in the prover-skeptic dialogue being mechanized. Lean on its own does not generate new proofs, so some generative program (i.e. a large language model) is required. On the other hand, without Lean performing the necessary skeptical role, there would be no way to verify the claims made by a large language model, at least not without an expenditure of human effort that OpenAI has neither the resources nor the interest to pursue.

Furthermore, formal verification using programs like Lean can be used to improve large language models, since the large language model can use feedback supplied by Lean to correct itself.

However, almost all headlines about AI progress in math have focused on the AI systems acting as the prover, and not nearly as much on Lean, which plays an unsung but equally essential skeptic role. As an aside, I am skeptical that other fields will see the same degree of progress made by AI in the near future, because verification of the output of generative AI systems cannot yet be efficiently mechanized in other fields. For example, there is no equivalent of Lean for oncology, so I believe that we are unlikely to see significant developments in cancer research being made by AI systems in the near future.

Why is a Lean certificate unsatisfying?

As I explained above, Lean is ridiculously good at being skeptical. Is a Lean certificate then to be taken as an infallible confirmation of a mathematical result? While there have been concerns raised about possible Lean kernel bugs, let us be generous and assume that a Lean certificate is an infallible confirmation of a theorem’s truth. That is, we will assume that if a type corresponding to a mathematical result has been instantiated in Lean, then the result is certainly true.

Even then, if a mathematician is seriously interested in a mathematical result, a Lean certificate on its own is unsatisfying. As explained above, it is an essential part of the methodology of mathematics to consider mathematical claims with skepticism, and this applies even if one believes the claims to be true.

This is in some ways a strange way to evaluate truth, and it is at odds with more everyday justifications for belief. For example, even though I have never studied its proof, I don’t really doubt Fermat’s Last Theorem in any practical sense, since its proof has been scrutinized by many experts in number theory. However, my belief in Fermat’s Last Theorem is justified only by an appeal to authority, so within a methodologically skeptical framework I do not know it to be true at all!

Thus practicing methodological skepticism sometimes involves make-believe. I will pretend not to believe in a theorem (even though I do believe it), in order to give myself the opportunity to be compelled to believe it. The process of being compelled to believe is what allows me to understand the theorem.

So sure, on some level I believe mathematical claims that are verified in Lean, even if I have not studied their proofs, but this is also basically an appeal to authority. From the perspective of methodological skepticism, I do not know that the results claimed by OpenAI are true until I have studied them and personally convinced myself that they are true.

Perhaps more substantially, it is impossible for a Lean certificate on its own to replace the role of skepticism explained by Bessis – skepticism as a process of interrogating and correcting one’s intuitions. Since a computer does not have access to our internal mental intuitions, there is no technological shortcut here. I am reminded of the famous statement attributed to Euclid, that “there is no royal road to geometry.” In one of many likely apocryphal stories about mathematicians from antiquity, it is said that he was responding to King Ptolemy’s question about whether there is an easier way to learn mathematics.

Recommendation

My recommendation is something that most mathematicians already practice: we should strive to use methodological skepticism to evaluate mathematical claims. This means that one should not believe a claim about mathematics unless personally convinced of its truth.

To be clear, this is an ideal from which I frequently fall short. Many mathematicians, including me, have a habit of using results “out of the tin” without understanding their proofs. However, I recognize that when I do this I am missing the mark. I tell myself that I will come back later and study the proofs of the results that I am using, and sometimes I actually follow through on that.

Since the coming of generative AI, we have seen large language models and Lean make progress in mathematics at a rate that is difficult or impossible to keep up with. Perhaps in the near future new and unbelievable mathematical results will be claimed that sound like they were lifted out of science fiction. These claims may be backed up by Lean certificates. Under these circumstances, it is important that we do not lose our heads. The practice of skepticism, of being able to say “I don’t know this to be true” will keep us grounded.

Acknowledgements

The author thanks Laurestine Bradford, Thomas B. Friedman, Anshula Gandhi, Patricia Marino, Yuveshen Mooroogen, as well as the editors at Proofs and Prompts for helpful comments on an earlier draft of the essay.

item.title: A vision of the future of mathematics
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts

item.content:encoded:
Florian Breuer1, Professor of mathematics at the University of Newcastle, Australia

AI Disclosure. This essay was revised after feedback from Claude Opus 5.5. Images generated by ChatGPT.

Math is hard

Mathematics has been struck by an asteroid. I don’t mean the nefarious action of a powerful corporation, but rather the empirical fact that AI systems are capable of superhuman mathematical ability. How this fact was revealed is not important; under different circumstances it may have been revealed sooner or later, or more gently, but ultimately the fact remains the same. We need to face it.

I think this fact reveals more about humans than about artificial intelligence. Humans are not very good at mathematics. It doesn’t come naturally to us and learning it is a slow, deliberate and (for many) painful process. Some never learn it at all. Our brains are not wired for mathematics; evolution never selected for it. What mathematical ability we do have is a side-effect of other, evolved abilities such as language and navigating a 3D world. Is it surprising that machines, trained first on the entirety of human mathematical knowledge, and then post-trained via RLVR2 on huge numbers of increasingly hard mathematical and coding problems, eventually learn to outperform us? The same happened with chess, and then Go. David Harvey3 points out that this means mathematics is only 30 years harder than chess (and 10 years harder than Go).

Why we did Mathematics

Much has been written about how the purpose of mathematics is, has always been and must remain the human understanding of mathematics. I’m not so sure.

We should examine why we do mathematics in the first place. The mathematical community is a diverse ecosystem of humans, and different members have different styles, abilities and motivations. Some are motivated by the pursuit of truth and beauty. Others live for the competitive thrill – to be smarter and better than others at this difficult activity. Yet others want to serve society by advancing the frontier of knowledge, leading to innovations which improve lives. Or we do it just because it’s enjoyable, and we’ve found a niche where we get paid for doing what we love. For most of us, it will be some combination of the above.4,5

So much for our own motivations; why should society support this activity, through salaries and grants? First, to teach. Mathematical thinking (problem solving, critical thinking, the ability to deal with abstraction), however puny in absolute terms, is highly valuable and transferable. As long as people need skills at all, this is among the skills they benefit most from learning. I also expect learning to remain a social activity – it requires almost superhuman willpower to push through the productive struggle needed to rewire your brain if you just study by yourself, with or without the help of AI tutors.

Just as importantly, mathematics underpins the other sciences and technology; it forms the wellspring of the famous innovation pipeline. Pure mathematics leads to applied mathematics leads to other sciences, finally to engineering and valuable technologies. One oft-quoted example is how centuries of number theory, the purest intellectual pursuit, led to public-key cryptography, without which the entire online economy could not function. We feel that even our most abstract and esoteric discoveries might one day, perhaps in 10 or 50 or 200 years, prove a vital input for an as-yet unimaginable new technology.

We grow indignant when those who pay us demand we demonstrate how our work will lead to immediate, real-world impact.

The future?

Many have written about how exciting the new mathematical future will be. Where we previously explored the alien landscape of mathematics on our hands and knees, we now get to drive around on AI-powered jeeps! After all, AI has only solved problem-solving and theorem-proving, which was never the point of mathematics (since mid-2026, anyway). Humans still ask the questions and build the new concepts. Peter Scholze is not yet obsolete, right?

Maybe AI will finally hit the skeptics’ wall,6 but I doubt it. If not, within the next year AIs will ask the better questions, build the more fruitful theories and push the mathematical frontier increasingly beyond our feeble human understanding.

The innovation pipeline will be supercharged. AIs that understand all of mathematics at once will spot applications that would never occur to one of us. They will convert these mathematical discoveries into new scientific insights and technological marvels with increasing speed and autonomy. The spigot at the end of the pipeline will become a cornucopia – if we live to see it.7 For the rest of society, this will be a good thing – just like weaving machines gave us cheaper clothes and the Luddites became a footnote of history. But human mathematicians can no longer cite the innovation pipeline in grant applications.

I predict that mathematics will crystallise into a database of formal statements and proofs, initially in Lean, but occasionally refactored as more suitable formal systems are invented. This monolith8 will grow outwards at a dizzying pace with no regard for human understanding. After all, the mathematicians and scientists using it won’t be human.

What will we, mere human mathematicians, do? We will probably keep teaching mathematics and mathematical thinking. Many of us will keep doing mathematics, human mathematics, fun and beautiful and insightful – and far from the frontier of knowledge. Some will mine the monolith (with AI help), and bring back shiny mathematical nuggets to digest and share. Others will close themselves off, jealously guarding their “Human Mathematics” from any AI contamination.

What, then, of the human understanding of mathematics? It is vital for teaching mathematical thinking, and will continue to bring us beauty and joy, but humans will no longer understand the research frontier.

Mathematics was fun when we were children and knew so much less than the adults. It was recreational and a valuable learning experience. We are about to relive this childhood.9 Can’t we just drop our conceits and status games and enjoy it?

What’s wrong with this picture?

The above vision of the future assumes the development of AI goes broadly well for humanity. This is an important assumption, and does not automatically hold unless we solve the alignment problem, which is hard.

The biggest problem with this vision is that in it we give up control of mathematics to the machines. This seems unavoidable, since the machines are so much better at it, and at producing the useful applications of it, than we are. This abdication will happen automatically, unless we somehow stop the development of powerful AI. The danger is that mathematics is not unique here – there are many domains in which AI will do better than humans, and for each domain individually it will seem rational to hand control to the more competent machines. Taken together, this leads to the gradual disempowerment of humanity. First, the machines came for the weavers – now they come for the rest of us. Scott Alexander argues that handing over to a perfectly aligned superintelligence may well be our best bet, but it is still extremely dangerous.

The vision also doesn’t address what we should do in the short term. Right now, for example, my university pays me to spend 40% of my time teaching, 40% on research and 20% on “service”. Setting aside the joke that my allocation is really 80-20-60, how can I justify 40% of my salary for what has become recreational mathematics? There are still research questions where a human + AI may be better than AI alone, and getting results is urgent, for example in post-quantum cryptography. In my case, I am learning to work on AI safety10 – I’m putting the transferability of my mathematical skills to the test.

But what of our students? The development of mathematical thinking skills is just as useful as ever, and the work of producing a thesis builds this – provided you don’t outsource this task to an AI. The value of a thesis is no longer the results therein (AI can produce these in an afternoon), but in the skills of the candidate. There are many places to put these skills to good use – starting with AI safety research. And if we do reach AI utopia, a lifetime of joyous mathematics awaits!

  1. My opinions are my own. Nevertheless, I benefited from conversations with David Harvey, Fabien Pazuki, Stephan Tornier and others. ︎
  2. Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards. ︎
  3. Private communication. ︎
  4. The pursuit of material gain, for money and power, is less common among mathematicians, since those who want these things, and find themselves with mathematical talent, can go work in finance and get rich. ︎
  5. Also, at least in my case, my sense of self-worth rests on my ability to do mathematics (however unremarkable by mathematicians’ standards). The recent developments are a bitter pill to swallow. ︎
  6. There is a theoretical barrier that AI progress is perpetually about to hit. It is always located slightly ahead of the current frontier, and has the unusual property of retreating at exactly the speed of approach. ︎
  7. Ensuring AI turns out well for humanity is the most important unsolved problem in the world now. Mathematicians have a role to play here, too! ︎
  8. Starting, perhaps, with the Tau Ceti Project. It may be surrounded by a larger cloud of less formal mathematics. ︎
  9. Assuming we can pay our bills! ︎
  10. I’m starting with a course at BlueDot. Other resources for mathematicians looking to get into AI safety research include MAISI, Iliad and the article Math for AI safety: an invitation for mathematicians by Lionel Levine. ︎

item.title: Positivist and Humanist Mathematics: A Case for Schism
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: If we do not split the discipline in two, one half of the discipline will inevitably dominate the other, and we will all be worse off for it. After all of the great crises of mathematics in which it survived as a whole, we now find ourselves in an entirely unprecedented situation. We either schism or die.
item.content:encoded:
Advith Govindarajan, PhD student at University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign

If intuitionism has been characterized with a certain propriety as revolutionists who overturned the ancien régime, Hilbert might be compared with Napoleon who, without regard for considerations of legitimacy, established, through a brilliant political stroke, a new order whose success is the substitute for legitimacy.
Kurt Grelling, 1928

And yet when one hears one of the greatest living mathematicians calmly telling the world that a considerable part of our analysis is devoid of proof, if not nonsense, and when one beholds the mighty efforts which the champions of Weierstrass are making to repel these attacks, it is reasonable, in view of such facts, to ask ourselves, ‘Is all well?’
James Pierpont, 1928

Taken from “Mystic, Geometer, and Intuitionist: The Life of L. E. J. Brouwer” by Dirk van Dalen

The discipline of Mathematics actualizes itself in the interstitial spaces between our research: in the coffee breaks during conferences, in the asides and footnotes in monographs, and in forum posts of mathematical communities. In those spaces we often hear and refer to the great crises of the past, of the crisis in euclidean geometry, of the crisis in foundations, of the crisis of formalism and constructivism. We now find ourselves in a new crisis which dominates the chatter of the collective coffee rooms of the world. Mathematics has been able to reconstitute itself from those past crises into a singular discipline; however I believe today the divisions are too deep to recover. I make a case for splitting the discipline into two: A positivist mathematics and a humanist mathematics, each with its own journals, institutions, faculty and norms.

There have always been two parts to our discipline. The first part, the positivist aspect of mathematics, entails formulating and proving theorems as its ultimate end goal. The second part, the humanist aspect of mathematics, entails the formulation of mathematical beauty and maturity as its ultimate end goal. These two parts have historically gone along hand-in-hand, with few eruptions. The humanist tradition of mathematics has been fruitful for the positivist end goals, and those positivist end goals have given direction and purpose to the humanist tradition. The current advances in AI technology now have broken this fruitful cooperation. We are reaching a stage where machines can now prove theorems, and we are not too far from the day where an engineer or scientist, needing grounding for a new theory or invention, can ask a machine to formulate the appropriate mathematical background and answer the relevant theorems.

There is of course, still a great need for humans in positivist mathematics: we still need humans to clean up proofs, to guide research directions, to act as the interface between the machines and their application. This is anathema to most humanist mathematicians: no longer would we be building towards mathematical beauty, but rather our discipline would be in some ways, ancillary to a greater project taken over by the machines. Personally, I fall in the humanist camp, but I think it is wrong to dismiss positivism entirely. The goal of positivist mathematics is certainly great: to facilitate the production and maintenance of the book of all the world’s greatest theorems. However, this goal is fundamentally incompatible with the way many of us want to do mathematics.

Some people wave away this incompatibility, arguing that we can square the difference: let humans work in theory formulation, and leave the rest up to the machines. It must be understood that this is already the positivist position. Indeed, it admits that our goal is the formulation of important theorems, and that our discipline should adapt itself to whatever new technologies are possible to achieve that goal. No one knows how far this technology will develop, but this attitude would see it that mathematicians continue to adapt as far as possible to those demands.

On the other hand, in the humanist viewpoint, we may see this as fundamentally absurd. The goal of humanist mathematics is the general development of the intellect. In this sense it shares allegiances with the arts and the humanities, even as it sometimes aids in the work of scientific discovery. Do we stop playing the piano just because digital synthesizers exist? Do we stop painting just because we have photography? Creating the most perfect, realistic image possible to capture the world is certainly a noble pursuit, but we should not let that stop us from engaging in the enterprise of painting as self-expression. By splitting mathematics in twain, both the positivists and humanists will find themselves more free. The positivists will be more free to pursue mathematics as a pure science, and the humanists will be more free to pursue mathematics as a form of beautiful self-expression.

To those reading this, imagine yourself on a hiring committee weighing two different job candidates. The first applicant has 30 papers. The papers are generally rough to read but answer some of the most important questions in the subfield. All their papers make very heavy use of the most advanced LLM technologies. They may answer poorly when asked to recall and explain much of their work but clearly understand intimately how to use LLMs to generate useful, important and interesting results. The second applicant has 5 papers, all human written. The questions they answer are small, some questions they answer are even already known! But the exposition in their papers is stunning and beautiful. When you interview them they are lively and demonstrate deep understanding and love of their work. Which candidate do you hire? The answer to this question determines where you fall along the positivist-humanist axis. It seems clear to me that these two candidates are working in fundamentally different disciplines and traditions, and that treating them in the same pool is a mistake.

If Mathematics does split along this division, it will be with some inevitable strife. Determining which departments, journals, conferences and institutions value the positivist endeavour and which ones value the humanist endeavour may require some bitter conflict. However, the disciplines that emerge from this conflict, Positivist Mathematics and Humanist Mathematics, will be stronger for it. If we do not make these decisions consciously, they will be made unconsciously for us. If we do not split the discipline in two, one half of the discipline will inevitably dominate the other, and we will all be worse off for it. After all of the great crises of mathematics in which it survived as a whole, we now find ourselves in an entirely unprecedented situation. We either schism or die.

item.title: On AI and Progress in Mathematics: Dreaming a Mathematical Universal Machine
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: Mathematics is moving from the mountain of solitary discovery to an industrial mine, where humans and AI explore together. What if mathematical progress were measured not by publications and citations, but by how much discoveries expand the capabilities of a Mathematical Universal Machine? A new vision of mathematical research.
item.content:encoded:
Vincent Runge, Associate Professor at Université d’Évry Paris-Saclay, Laboratoire de Mathématiques et Modélisation d’Évry (LaMME)

Mathematicians often like to describe their research with the metaphor of climbing a mountain. Through an immense solitary effort, we reach a summit from which we contemplate a vast landscape of unexplored mathematical truths. From the mountain, we have now descended into the mine: an industrial landscape filled with machines, unexpected discoveries, and disruptive innovations. The romance of the search, the ideal of pen and paper, in which human genius could win immense fame through solitary effort alone, has been lost along the way. As John von Neumann once wrote, “For progress, there is no cure” (“Can We Survive Technology?”, Fortune, 1955): we have no choice but to adapt.

Soon, we will all be miners digging in the mathematical mine, either collaborating or competing with mathematical AI machines. Publications would then be seen primarily as a means of helping humans understand mathematics, while the measurement of mathematical progress would be entrusted to a Mathematical Universal Machine.

This post summarizes the ideas of my recent preprint, which explores what this brave new world of mathematics might look like and how we might collectively shape its future.

What we are afraid to lose

Year after year, we patiently build our own little planet of mathematics. We explore it with constant effort, and these explorations produce stories as well as theorems. The living experience of mathematics lies in sharing what we have learned: passing on intuitions, mistakes, and the secret gestures of mathematical thinking. All of this, and much more, is the human adventure of mathematics. With AI, we risk becoming the Geographer of Saint-Exupéry’s Le Petit Prince, who never leaves his desk: we would let the AI explore the planet for us. The AI would be much faster, much more efficient, and more accurate. But we would lose the pleasure of exploration: choosing where to go, with all its approximations and errors.

We were trained to prove, and proof itself risks becoming obsolete as a distinctively human skill. When proofs become abundant, where is the new scarcity? There is a second danger. Mathematics rests on unusually strong norms of trust and intellectual honesty, and AI risks releasing one of the worst genies from the bottle: suspicion. A divide between the “AI-free” and the “AI-assisted” mathematician could fracture our community.

Decoupling understanding from measurement

The old system of papers, peer review, journals, citations and prestige was never perfect; faced with an abundance of machine-generated mathematics, it may become increasingly inadequate. I propose to partially decouple the advancement of human understanding from the measurement of mathematical progress. Publications would serve primarily to help humans understand mathematics, while progress would be measured by a new institution: a Mathematical Universal Machine (MUM), a shared AI infrastructure available to the entire mathematical community, in the spirit of H.G. Wells’s World Brain (1938).

The mine and the miner

Let me make the metaphor of the mathematical mine more precise. The mine is the space of mathematical truth, results are diamonds hidden within it, and proofs are the tunnels leading to them. The mathematical AI system is the miner, M=(θ,K,T)M=(\theta,\mathcal K,\mathcal T), with three components:

  • maps K\mathcal K: research papers, databases of proven results, definitions, graphs of dependencies between theorems;
  • tools T\mathcal T: Lean for formal verification, Python and computer algebra for experimentation;
  • a brain θ\theta: a large language model, with a memory of its past attempts, which decides where and how to dig.

The miner has finite patience, represented by a finite computational budget BB: the resources of the Machine must ultimately be shared among all mathematicians. More fundamentally, I believe that designing the Machine itself could become a new goal of mathematical research: building a system that achieves the highest possible rate of discovery per budget, or of energy.

Left to explore freely, the Machine progressively fills in the territory accessible from what is already known: I call this the convexification of the mine. My hypothesis is that human intelligence and imagination will not be entirely subsumed by the Machine: new viewpoints, unexpected definitions and genuinely original research may lie outside this convexification. This suggests two complementary modes of research:

  • the mathematician as a supervisor, who explores mathematics through the Machine, proposing directions and steering the miner within their own expertise;
  • the mathematician as a miner, who works outside the Machine to reach mathematics beyond its current horizon. The resulting papers become new maps which, through a Machine Update, change how the miner explores.

Measuring progress: the Machine horizon

For a statement TT known to humans but excluded from the Machine’s prior knowledge, let pM(T∣B)p_M(T\mid B) be the probability that the miner proves TT within the budget BB. For a level p∈(0,1)p\in(0,1), the Machine horizon is the set of results the Machine can reach:

HM(B;p)={T:pM(T∣B)≥p}.\mathcal H_M(B;p)=\{T : p_M(T\mid B)\ge p\}.

The Machine would be updated at fixed intervals with newly published mathematics, θt→θt+1\theta_t\to\theta_{t+1}, and its capabilities reassessed after each update: how much a contribution raises the probabilities of success, enlarges the horizon, or reduces the computation needed to reach a result. Such measurements could complement peer review and provide a new basis for recognizing the contributions of mathematicians, whether they discover new mathematics themselves or improve the Machine’s exploration as supervisors. This echoes Erdős’s book (see Aigner and Ziegler’s Proofs from THE BOOK): rather than collecting the most beautiful proof of each theorem, I propose to seek shorter paths to entire regions of the mine. The goal would be to design a Mathematical Universal Machine with the fastest possible discovery rate, the ratio of mathematical capacity to computational budget (or energy) becoming the new metric.

A political project

The current trajectory of AI is not what we dreamed of. It consumes considerable amounts of energy, water, land, and physical resources. It raises serious ethical concerns when associated with surveillance, social control or warfare. Moreover, AI for mathematics is concentrated in the hands of a few private companies, whose most powerful models are accessible only to selected collaborators. We must not resign ourselves to this status quo. We can build a universal AI infrastructure for mathematics, developed in partnership with an international institution such as UNESCO, governed by mathematicians (for instance through the International Mathematical Union), and belonging to the global scientific commons. As a starting point, it could follow six principles:

  • Ecological accountability: its energy consumption and environmental footprint independently assessed and published every year.
  • Open architecture: the model architecture, its weights, and the essential components of the system openly accessible.
  • Universal and equal access: open to the whole mathematical community, students included, with an equal computational budget for every user.
  • Privacy: private research and unpublished results never incorporated into the shared system without explicit consent.
  • Transparent Machine Updates: a yearly update with newly published mathematics, together with an estimate of the computational importance of each contribution.
  • International scientific governance: a joint mathematics and computer science laboratory responsible for updates, maintenance, evaluation and communication.

Life in the mine

Asked what percentage of mathematics one could hope to understand, John von Neumann reportedly answered “about 28 percent”. With the Machine, we might recover something of the nineteenth-century ideal of understanding mathematics as a whole. I do not want to sound naively optimistic: this text deliberately takes a positive stance, while the reality is challenging, frightening and even depressing. But in the mud of the mine, we still have the power to organize the search collectively: adaptation is not optional (for progress, there is no cure), but preserving our values, and some of our working habits, is still possible.

AI disclosure. This post was condensed from my preprint with the help of an AI, which drafted a first version of the text; the ideas are my own.

item.title: Working with the AI Companies is a Losing Strategy
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: I’ll agree that it was worth a shot, but working with AI companies got us essentially nothing and now it’s time for a different approach.
item.content:encoded:
Anonymous, Assistant Professor (no tenure) from North America.

In response to Open AI’s October 6th release of hundreds of results, the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence (AGMAI) released a statement saying, “it is ultimately up to the mathematical community to assess the extent to which our recommendations were followed successfully.” By far the most important recommendation that AGMAI had made was for AI companies to stop “testing advanced mathematical problems on proprietary models that remain inaccessible to the broader scientific community.” They identify the obvious reasons for this: it concentrates control over a powerful means of production of mathematical results in the hands of whoever has access to the best models and the most compute, so essentially the AI companies and whoever they decide grant access to. While OpenAI has offered some conciliatory words and paltry financial resources, they explicitly said from the outset that they have no intention of listening to AGMAI on the core issue of testing open problems on internal models. Thus, I conclude that AGMAI’s recommendations were not followed in any substantive fashion, and that AI companies have no intention of changing this in the future. I’ll agree that it was worth a shot, but working with AI companies got us essentially nothing and now it’s time for a different approach. As a start, AGMAI should dissolve itself rather than continue to provide a veneer of legitimacy to OpenAI while OpenAI ignores their central recommendation.

Right now, mathematicians still have some influence because we have things the AI companies want: our data and the legitimacy of our mathematical institutions. The latter is why OpenAI bothered forming AGMAI in the first place. When we work with commercial AI to solve problems, we provide AI companies with valuable training data. In some cases, access to this data might even allow AI companies to solve these problems first using more powerful internal models and without properly crediting the work they built on: behavior that would be condemned as academic dishonesty if you or I did it. When we cite commercial AI services in our papers, we provide free advertising for AI companies. When we tell the media that OpenAI’s release of results is exciting and a big advance for mathematics, we legitimize their unethical research practices. The more we do these things, the more we strengthen the position of AI companies and weaken our own with respect to deciding the future of mathematics. We should stop and seriously ask ourselves if this is what we want to do.

A counterargument is that if we continue to work with AI companies, we can persuade them to adopt norms more aligned with those of the mathematical community. Beyond their behavior thus far, I find this unlikely because the AI companies and many of those associated with them have been quite forthcoming about their beliefs and vision for the future, and if I take them at their word, I can’t see things leading anywhere positive for the existing mathematical community. Many AI company employees (and some mathematicians) sincerely believe that what they are doing has a nonnegligible probability of literally killing everyone, yet they race ahead and implicitly believe themselves justified in making the choice to do so on behalf of humanity. OpenAI’s October 6th release reeks of the Silicon Valley “move fast and break things” ethos, where a private company acts recklessly and destructively to capture value for itself while leaving others to clean up the resulting messes. Also along these lines, recently released documents reveal that insiders at OpenAI believed they were acting unethically and in some cases illegally by scraping training data and using it for their own profit without asking consent from or providing compensation to the humans who produced the data, yet they continue to operate in this manner. Anthropic talks a big game about safety while privately shopping a toothless safety bill that would insulate them from regulation. Sam Altman uses the language of effective altruism to justify near-term harm for the vague promise of a future of material abundance, often eliding the fact that in this future AI companies would amass sweeping control over the means of production, in our context of mathematical results, but aspirationally of all economic value. Are these the people and institutions we want to decide the future of mathematics, let alone of society at large?

There might still be time. If we unite, organize, and exert our influence against the harmful practices of AI companies, we can defend our institutions and community. Imagine if we had all collectively responded to OpenAI’s October 6th release by rejecting the legitimacy of OpenAI’s unethical research practices rather than with shell-shocked chaos. Sure, the preprints they produced would still exist, but I believe this would have had a powerful effect. And maybe AI companies say they don’t need us (their ultimate goal either way) and that they will build their own mathematics. Then we should make them do so without mathematicians or mathematical institutions.

Note too, that opposing AI companies doesn’t mean we need to disavow AI. Many mathematicians have written thoughtfully, here and elsewhere, about how we can harness the potential of AI to advance our understanding of mathematics while ensuring a healthy future for our human communities. Tao and others have written about the need for us to build our own AI infrastructure in which we can ensure equitable access and proper attribution. We should make this a priority so that we are not dependent on the AI companies, and once we have achieved this, we can reap the rewards. However each of us feels about the use of AI in mathematics research personally, we now exist in a world in which AI can accelerate mathematical progress. Opposing AI companies is not about pretending the technology doesn’t exist or that it won’t have an impact. Rather, it is about recognizing that the survival of our institutions and communities depends on our political choices just as much as our mathematical and philosophical choices. As Tao recently stated, mathematics is now on a “war footing,” and if we choose poorly, we will lose the war.

I know firsthand that this is a difficult ask. For one, opposing the AI companies can feel hopeless because they are already so rich and powerful. They promote a narrative of inevitability and want us to feel this way, but we can at least find out for ourselves if it’s true rather than preemptively give up. Another challenge is that many of us have responded thus far in the ways we did because we sincerely love mathematics and discovery rather than out of any intention to aid the AI companies. When I hear a major problem in my field has been resolved, my first instincts are toward excitement and curiosity. I want to come together with colleagues to celebrate a milestone and unpack the new ideas, questions, and directions opened by the advance. Even though the October 6th release was hundreds of slop papers, there are almost certainly insights to be gleaned, and for some of us, to set this aside goes against our integrity as mathematicians and scientists. But right now, that is what we must do to survive. If we allow ourselves to become distracted by shiny new theorems and paltry donations while our institutions are captured and our future generations live in fear for their livelihoods, then the future of mathematics will be written by AI companies rather than mathematicians.

Received October 26.

item.title: Sharing two worries about AI
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: First, the ill-effects of AI on my personal mathematical experience. If widely shared, they could have a long-term pernicious influence on the subject as a whole. Second, I put this in the context of the larger threats AI poses to the human world. These are not nested problems: they are parallel.
item.content:encoded:
David Solomon, Chercheur associé at Institut de Mathématiques de Jussieu

I am not as optimistic as some posting on this site, either about the long term effects of AI on Maths or its effects on the world as a whole. I hope I’m wrong. Here are my worries:

1) First, let me state two major activities that I really enjoy when I’m doing maths and which provide much of my motivation to do it. Neither should seem strange to the majority of human mathematicians, whether ‘professional’ or amateur but I want to restate them clearly in this context:

a) Finding a problem from which a creative project is born, creating a suitable framework for my approach, checking it, querying it, tussling with the problems and (hopefully) eventually arriving at something satisfying. That’s a great feeling we must all know. It’s a reward for our creation, hard work and solitary reflection. It may also show a new path forward as well, perhaps to other existing problems, or reveal questions that intrigue me…

b) Discussing my ideas with other (need I say “human”?) mathematicians, partly to show off my creations (yes!) and partly to share and partly to get their input (new viewpoints, questions context etc) during the process. Maybe even find a link to what they’re doing in their work. As well as verbal discussion, I might send an email or a preprint on a partial result or maybe an account of my ideas or possible spin-offs. I might also put one on ArXiv or try to publish it in a journal.

The problem: unfortunately, as things stand with AI at the present time, I can’t help feeling that indulging in (b) may compromise my ability to enjoy (a): if someone takes my ideas and feeds them into an LLM or if the same LLM is directed to scrape the internet for papers on a certain topic that can help it solve a similar problem someone has proposed to it, and if it comes across my ideas, in that case I risk being deprived of much of the satisfaction described in (a): not only the “glory” of solving (probably a reprehensible desire and quite possibly unachievable anyway) but also the pleasures of tussling and creating.

So, at present I am thinking that I need to stop doing (b), or do it much less and more guardedly, for the sake of (a). Some take a more “selfless” attitude in this respect (or seem to), but I can’t be alone in feeling that I need to prioritise (a) otherwise I will experience frustration and, ultimately, lose motivation for either. This is not a good situation for me and, if many people react like me, it won’t have a good effect on the subject either. So how do we tackle it? Can we?

2) Secondly, I don’t think there has been quite enough focus in the discussions here on setting the problems AI is causing for academic mathematics in the context of the larger and – let’s say it clearly – much more worrying problems that it threatens to cause the human world as a whole. I would like to point out that these two issues are far from being unconnected. Neither is the first simply a minor corollary of the second: Obviously there will be no human mathematics if there are no humans to do it but, less dramatically, in both areas, the main threat is a loss of human control over human activities, whether that control is given away, lost by accident or stolen for ulterior motives by certain actors, possibly (but not necessarily) silicon ones. In this sense the present anxiety of mathematicians for their subject can be seen as a useful illustration of the larger problems we may all be facing pretty soon.
